planting.note: Direct sow into warm, sandy soil once all frost danger has passed, spacing hills widely to let the sprawling vines run.

directions: This is the wild citron melon landrace of the Kalahari Desert, long relied upon by San and Khoisan communities as a seasonal water source for both people and livestock during the dry season. Unlike dessert watermelons the hard white flesh is rarely eaten raw, since many fruits carry a bitter compound, and is instead boiled down into preserves, added to stews, or fed to animals, while the oil-rich seeds are roasted or pressed. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once the long taproot establishes, needs full sun and very little supplemental water, and sprawls across open ground the way a feral watermelon would. Save seed from sweeter, less bitter fruits if selecting a line for home garden preserving use.

planting.note: Direct sow shelled seed into loose, well-drained soil after the soil has warmed, since the pegs that form pods need to penetrate easily into the ground.

directions: Named for the Chalimbana research station in Zambia, this large-kerneled Virginia-type groundnut is one of the most widely grown smallholder peanut landraces across Zambia, Malawi, and neighboring Mozambique. After its small yellow pea-like flowers self-pollinate, the pegs elongate downward and bury the developing pods in the soil, so loose, sandy loam and consistent moisture during pegging noticeably improve yield. The large, flavorful kernels are a staple boiled or roasted snack and are ground into the thick groundnut stews and relishes common in southern African cooking. It needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature, so gardeners in cooler climates should treat it as a full-season crop started as soon as the soil is reliably warm.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out only once nights stay reliably warm, since this pepper sulks in cool soil.

directions: Shombo is the slim, finger-length chili widely sold in Nigerian markets and distinguished from the rounder ata rodo (scotch bonnet type) by its milder, grassier heat and elongated shape. It is a staple seasoning pepper in Yoruba and broader Nigerian cooking, typically blended fresh into pepper sauces, stews, and jollof-style dishes rather than dried. The compact, bushy plant produces heavily over a long season and appreciates consistent warmth and even moisture, with light afternoon shade helping fruit set in the hottest climates. Harvest pods green for a milder flavor or let them ripen to red for a fuller, slightly sweeter heat.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and set out rooted plants against a trellis or fence once the weather is reliably warm.

directions: Utazi, also called arokeke among the Yoruba, is a bitter-leaved climbing vine central to Igbo and broader southern Nigerian cooking, where a few finely shredded young leaves are stirred into dishes like ofe nsala (white soup) or scattered raw over isi ewu as a sharp, aromatic garnish. It is almost always propagated from stem cuttings rather than seed, rooting readily in warm, humid conditions before being planted out near a trellis, fence, or small tree it can climb. The vine prefers filtered light to full sun, consistently moist but well-drained soil, and regular harvesting of young growth which encourages continued branching. In frost-free climates it persists for years as a perennial, while in cooler regions it is best grown as a container vine brought in before cold weather.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products
